title: Evaluating Technical Options
description: Learn how to systematically compare technology choices using structured evaluation frameworks, decision matrices, and proof-of-concept validation.

data.text: Every senior engineer faces technical choices: which database to use, whether to build or buy, how to architect a new service. Making these decisions well separates good engineers from great ones. Evaluating options is not about finding the perfect solution — it is about finding the best fit for your specific context.

A good evaluation balances facts with judgment. You will never have complete information, and that is okay. The goal is to reduce uncertainty enough to make a confident choice, then commit and move forward.

Before evaluating solutions, write down exactly what problem you are solving. A vague problem statement like "we need a better database" leads to vague decisions. A clear statement like "we need a database that handles 10,000 writes per second with sub-100ms read latency and automatic failover" gives you concrete criteria to evaluate against.

data.title: The One-Sentence Test
data.text: If you cannot explain the problem in one or two sentences to someone outside your team, you are not ready to evaluate solutions. Write it down, share it, and refine it until it is crystal clear.

Start broad, then narrow. List every plausible option, even ones that seem unlikely. This prevents you from overlooking a better solution because you jumped to the first familiar answer. Typical categories include: build internally, use an open-source tool, adopt a managed cloud service, or buy a commercial product.

data.title: Generating a Shortlist: Authentication
data.content: When evaluating how to add user authentication to a new web application:
data.code:
Problem: Add secure user authentication with social login

Broad list:
1. Build custom auth with JWT and OAuth libraries
2. Use Firebase Authentication
3. Use Auth0
4. Use AWS Cognito
5. Use Passport.js with local strategy
6. Use NextAuth.js
7. Use Okta

Narrowed shortlist (after 30-minute discussion):
- NextAuth.js (team already uses Next.js)
- Auth0 (enterprise features, generous free tier)
- Firebase Auth (already use Firebase for hosting)

Discarded without deep analysis:
- Custom JWT (maintenance burden too high)
- Okta (cost too high for current stage)

data.text: A weighted decision matrix forces objectivity. List your evaluation criteria, assign each a weight from 1 to 5 based on importance, then score each option from 1 to 5 on each criterion. Multiply weight by score and sum the results. The highest total score wins — but always sanity-check the result against your intuition.

data.title: Weighted Decision Matrix: API Gateway
data.content: Evaluating API gateway options for a growing SaaS platform.
data.code:
Criteria              | Weight | Kong | AWS API GW | Envoy | NGINX
----------------------|--------|------|------------|-------|-------
Performance           |   5    |  3   |     4      |   5   |   5
Cost                  |   4    |  4   |     3      |   5   |   5
Team Expertise        |   5    |  2   |     4      |   3   |   4
Ecosystem             |   4    |  4   |     5      |   4   |   3
Rate Limiting         |   3    |  5   |     4      |   5   |   3
OAuth Integration     |   3    |  3   |     5      |   3   |   2
----------------------|--------|------|------------|-------|-------
Weighted Score        |        | 62   |    76      |  68   |  70

Winner: AWS API Gateway — strongest ecosystem and OAuth support,
which matters most for our SaaS use case.

data.text: When the decision is high-stakes, build a proof of concept. A good proof of concept answers a specific question rather than trying to build production-ready software. Timebox it to one or two weeks, measure real performance against your requirements, and document what you learned — even if the result is inconclusive.

data.title: Proof of Concept Checklist
data.content: Use this checklist when planning a proof of concept.
data.code:
PoC Planning:

1. Define the exact question to answer
   - Example: "Can PostgreSQL handle 50K writes/sec with partitioning?"

2. Identify success criteria before starting
   - Example: "Sustained throughput above 45K writes/sec"

3. Timebox the effort (1-2 weeks maximum)

4. Use realistic data volumes and traffic patterns

5. Measure the right metrics
   - Latency (p50, p95, p99)
   - Throughput (requests per second)
   - Resource usage (CPU, memory, network)

6. Document findings, not just code
   - What worked
   - What surprised you
   - What you would do differently

7. Make a clear recommendation or next step

data.text: Data informs decisions, but intuition plays a role too. If the weighted matrix says one thing and your experience says another, pause and investigate. Intuition often captures tacit knowledge — patterns you have seen before but have not yet articulated. The goal is to understand why your intuition disagrees, not to ignore it.

terms.definition: A structured comparison tool that scores options against weighted criteria to produce an objective ranking.
A timeboxed, minimal implementation designed to answer a specific technical question.
The measurable attributes — such as performance, cost, and maintainability — used to judge technical options.

data.title: Avoid Analysis Paralysis
data.text: Set a hard deadline for decisions. Perfect information is never available, and delaying a good decision often costs more than making a slightly suboptimal one. If you have enough information to be 80 percent confident, that is usually enough to commit.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Write a clear, one-paragraph problem statement before evaluating any solution
Start with a broad list of options, then narrow to a shortlist of three to five
Use weighted decision matrices to add objectivity to subjective choices
Run timeboxed proof of concepts for high-stakes decisions
Trust your intuition, but always investigate why it disagrees with the data
Document the criteria, scores, and rationale so others can follow your reasoning
data.takeaway: Structured evaluation reduces bias, surfaces hidden assumptions, and builds confidence in technical decisions.
